claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr can be maintained as a single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloy.
Rapid cooling or suitable thermodynamic conditions can stabilize the bcc HfNbTaTiZr state against transformation or phase separation.
The initial single-phase bcc alloy has a random solid-solution distribution at high temperature.
Controlled intermediate-temperature annealing will evolve SRO from isolated clusters into a percolating network while retaining the single-phase bcc structure.
The relevant transport regime has a phonon mean free path comparable to the spacing between SRO clusters.
Prior refractory-alloy simulations can impose a fixed-SRO approximation that neglects dynamic ordering.
An appropriate potential-energy surface must permit dynamic SRO evolution to represent the proposed transport regime.
Percolating chemically ordered clusters create a continuous pathway for phonon propagation that is distinct from isolated clusters.
Before percolation, isolated SRO clusters behave like point defects and initially reduce thermal conductivity through phonon scattering.
Connectivity of the SRO clusters reduces the effective scattering cross-section for long-wavelength phonons.
Phonons traveling through connected ordered regions experience reduced Umklapp or boundary scattering.
Once SRO clusters percolate, thermal conductivity increases or remains anomalously high because the connected network bypasses scattering mechanisms associated with isolated clusters.
Thermal conductivity will show an inflection or non-monotonic dependence on annealing time or temperature, with an initial decrease followed by an increase or plateau.
Serial or parallel mixing models and point-defect scattering theories predict a monotonic conductivity reduction as SRO volume fraction increases.
The predicted conductivity behavior will deviate from serial or parallel mixing-model predictions because those models do not account for topological percolation.
If annealing causes phase separation into phases such as Laves or B2, the proposed percolative mechanism no longer applies.
If SRO clusters remain below the percolation threshold, conventional scattering-induced conductivity reduction will dominate.
Accurate potential-energy surfaces capable of capturing SRO dynamics are currently lacking for these refractory systems.
The phonon dispersion within a percolating SRO network has not been fully characterized for the specified refractory alloy systems.
A connectivity value greater than 0.5 is sufficient to establish that the SRO clusters have percolated.
